title: “YOUR BREASTS ARE LIKE CLUSTERS OF FRUIT”: The Song of Songs Passage Many Christians Never Hear Read Aloud
paragraphs: “YOUR BREASTS ARE LIKE CLUSTERS OF FRUIT”: The Song of Songs Passage Many Christians Never Hear Read Aloud
We are comfortable saying God created the human body—until the Bible starts talking about it.
Verses we print on coffee mugs, place over sunsets, memorize with our children, whisper beside hospital beds, and post when life falls apart.
And then there are verses like this.
Verses that make the room suddenly uncomfortable.
Verses a preacher may read faster than the others.
Verses that make some Christians wonder, for half a second, whether somebody accidentally slipped the wrong book into the Bible.
“Your breasts are like clusters of fruit.”
And the Hebrew is not embarrassed.
זֹאת קוֹמָתֵךְ דָּמְתָה לְתָמָר וְשָׁדַיִךְ לְאַשְׁכֹּלוֹת
Zot qomatekh damtah letamar, veshadayikh le’ashkolot.
“Your stature is like a palm tree, and your breasts like clusters.”

The Hebrew word שָׁדַיִךְ (shadayikh) really does mean “your breasts.” The word אֶשְׁכּוֹלוֹת (eshkolot) means “clusters.” The comparison to the palm tree is right there in the Hebrew text. This is not an embarrassing mistranslation modern Christians need to rescue God from. It belongs to the poetry of Song of Songs itself.
And the next line becomes even more intimate:
אָמַרְתִּי אֶעֱלֶה בְתָמָר אֹחֲזָה בְּסַנְסִנָּיו וְיִהְיוּ־נָא שָׁדַיִךְ כְּאֶשְׁכְּלוֹת הַגֶּפֶן
Amarti e’eleh vetamar, ochazah besansinnav; veyihyu-na shadayikh ke’eshkelot hagefen...
“I said, ‘I will climb the palm tree; I will take hold of its branches. May your breasts be like clusters of the vine...’”
The Hebrew text really is that direct. The following imagery speaks of fragrance, apples, wine, desire, and the lovers belonging to one another.
And perhaps the first lesson is embarrassingly simple.
God is not embarrassed by what God created.
Somewhere along the way, many Christians learned a strange equation.
Holiness means pretending bodies do not exist.
Purity means never speaking about desire.
Spiritual maturity means becoming uncomfortable whenever Scripture becomes physical.
But then you open the Bible...
Not lust stripped of covenant, dignity, and personhood.
A man beholding the woman he loves.
A woman speaking her own desire.
Two lovers celebrating one another with the vocabulary of gardens, vineyards, fruit, fragrance, wine, spices, flowers, gazelles, palms, and pomegranates.
And suddenly our embarrassment says more about us than it does about Scripture.
Maybe you were raised to believe that anything involving the human body was automatically dirty.
You heard sermons warning you about lust—which Scripture rightly warns against—but almost never heard anyone explain that sexual desire itself was not invented by pornography.
God created humanity male and female before Genesis ever introduced the serpent.
And Genesis says something astonishing about that original world: the man and woman were naked and were not ashamed.
And one of the first things humanity did was hide.
Because shame has been whispering ever since.
Then Jesus walks into human history looking for people hiding behind trees all over again.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because it matters so much that He came to save sinners from it.
There is an enormous difference between biblical sexuality and the counterfeit sexuality sold by our culture.
Pornography takes a person and turns that person into a product.
Biblical love asks, “How can I cherish?”
Pornography disconnects the body from covenant, responsibility, sacrifice, and personhood.
The beloved is not merely anatomy.
She belongs to her beloved, and her beloved belongs to her.
Just a few verses after this passage comes one of the Song’s most important declarations:
“I am my beloved’s, and his desire is for me.”
She is not presented as a disposable body.
She is not merely being looked at.
She belongs within a relationship of mutual delight.
And perhaps that is why Song of Songs makes both religious shame and modern sexual consumerism uncomfortable.
It refuses to say the body is filthy.
And it refuses to say the body is merchandise.
It gives us something far more beautiful.
Bodies without shame becoming bodies without boundaries.
Passion that still recognizes a person.
And that distinction desperately matters now.
Because some people reading this have spent years believing Christianity's answer to sexual brokenness was simply:
But Jesus came for something deeper than behavioral suppression.
Christianity does not merely announce that certain desires must be resisted.
It announces that the entire human person can be redeemed.
Maybe pornography has trained your eyes to consume instead of cherish.
Maybe sexual sin became the secret room of your life.
Promise God it was the last time.
And afterward comes the familiar silence.
The moment when temptation has finished making promises and shame arrives to collect the bill.
Maybe affection was weaponized against you.
Maybe the word “intimacy” does not make you smile.
It makes something inside you tighten.
Maybe religious people handed you shame for wounds somebody else caused.
Maybe you learned to hate the mirror.
Maybe you have spent years believing that what happened to your body somehow changed your worth.
And maybe you have wondered whether God could possibly look at all of it without turning away.
The Christ of Christianity is not a distant spirit floating safely above human suffering.
God the Son entered human embodiment.
A Roman scourge tore His flesh.
His body was placed in a tomb.
And Christianity does not end with Jesus escaping His body.
Christian hope is not ultimately the liberation of good souls from disgusting bodies.
It is redemption so complete that Scripture points toward resurrection.
Christ is making all things new.
That means your body is neither your god nor your garbage.
It is not something to worship.
It is not something to despise.
It belongs under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
And this is where Song of Songs becomes unexpectedly confrontational.
Because if your theology can only deal with souls and cannot deal with bodies, your theology is too small.
If your Christianity knows how to condemn lust but does not know how to describe holy love, something is missing.
If churches teach teenagers everything sex can destroy but never explain what covenant love was meant to protect, something is missing.
And if Christians are more embarrassed by biblical marital desire than the world is by pornography, something has gone terribly wrong.
Song of Songs will not let us pretend God is afraid of His own creation.
But neither will the rest of Scripture let us baptize every desire merely because we feel it.
That is the tension mature Christianity must be willing to hold.
And Jesus is Lord over all of it.
That may be the part that hurts.
Because sometimes we want Jesus as Savior while keeping locked rooms where He is not allowed to be Lord.
And Christ stands before the room we have spent years protecting.
Not because He wants to humiliate us.
Repentance is not God screaming, “You are disgusting.”
Repentance is the terrifying mercy of God saying:
“You don't have to live here anymore.”
Bring the relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
Bring the wounds you covered with pleasure.
Bring the hunger underneath the habit.
Bring the thing you promised yourself nobody would ever know.
Bring all of it into the light.
Because grace is not permission to remain enslaved.
Grace is Christ meeting sinners where they actually are and refusing to leave them there.
Forgiveness is offered not because we finally became clean enough to approach Him, but because His blood is sufficient to cleanse those who come to Him in repentance and faith.
The scandal is not that sinners need grace.
The scandal is how far Grace came to find us.
Maybe that is why this strange, beautiful, uncomfortable passage belongs in our Bibles.
It reminds us that Christianity is not frightened by reality.
The Bible does not need us to sanitize humanity before God is allowed into the room.
So maybe the question after reading Song of Songs 7 is not:
“Why would God allow language like this into Scripture?”
“Why did we become so uncomfortable with a God who refuses to abandon any part of human existence to darkness?”
Your sexuality does not need another counterfeit savior.
Your shame does not need another hiding place.
Your loneliness does not need another temporary anesthetic.
Your wounds do not need another mask.
Not a sanitized Christ who only appears in church buildings.
The Savior who tells sinners to repent and then gives repentant sinners something shame never could:
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to describe your private sin publicly. But you can make a simple declaration that refuses secrecy's power.

And if somebody came into your mind while reading this—someone carrying sexual shame, someone recovering from pornography, someone who thinks Christianity hates the human body, someone who has been wounded, someone trying to rebuild a marriage, someone who desperately needs to discover the difference between condemnation and conviction—send this to them.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends who are willing to listen.

Scripture recognizes the legitimacy of materially supporting those who labor in Gospel ministry—Paul writes that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive their living from the Gospel. But Scripture is equally clear that Christian giving must never be manipulated: each person should give as he has decided in his heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion.” Give first where conscience, Scripture, and faithful stewardship before God lead you.
Send it privately to someone who needs it.
Pray for the people who will encounter it.
Because sometimes the post you almost did not share becomes the sentence someone reads at 2:13 in the morning while deciding whether they are too dirty to come home to God.
They are not beyond the reach of Christ.
Because the final word over a surrendered life is not the browser history.
Not what somebody did to you.
The final word belongs to Jesus.
What shame tells you to bury, Jesus calls into the light—not to destroy you, but to begin writing what you thought could never be redeemed.
